spt-rugby-first-international.why: A football match billed as England against Scotland had been played in London in 1870, but under association rules and with a Scottish side drawn from London residents. Scottish rugby clubs objected and issued a public challenge to play England under rugby rules. The Rugby Football Union had been formed only weeks earlier.
spt-rugby-first-international.impact: The match became an annual fixture and encouraged the Scots to form their own union in 1873. Ireland and Wales soon joined the international calendar, laying the ground for the Home Nations Championship. Teams were cut from twenty players to fifteen in 1877, which opened up the game.

spt-fa-cup-final.why: The Football Association, founded in 1863, still had few member clubs and competing local rules. Its secretary Charles Alcock proposed a knockout challenge cup in 1871, modelled on the house matches he had known at Harrow School. Fifteen clubs entered the first competition, most of them from the London area.
spt-fa-cup-final.impact: The cup gave clubs a reason to play under one set of rules and helped association football spread across Britain. In the 1880s professional sides from northern and Midland towns displaced the gentleman amateurs who had won the early finals. Its knockout format was copied by cup competitions around the world.

spt-first-test-match.why: English professional teams had toured Australia since the 1860s, usually playing local sides that fielded extra men to even the odds. By the time James Lillywhite brought his team out in 1876, colonial cricket had improved enough for a combined New South Wales and Victoria eleven to meet the tourists on equal terms.
spt-first-test-match.impact: England won a return match a fortnight later, and tours in both directions soon became regular. Australia's win in England in 1882 gave rise to the Ashes. Matches between national sides came to be treated as the highest form of cricket, and other countries were gradually admitted to Test status.

spt-wimbledon.why: Lawn tennis was a new craze. Major Walter Wingfield had marketed a boxed version of the game in 1874, and it quickly overtook croquet on the lawns of the British middle classes. The All England club added tennis in 1875 and had to settle a common set of rules before it could hold a tournament.
spt-wimbledon.impact: The rules drawn up for the tournament, including the rectangular court and the scoring borrowed from real tennis, became the basis of the modern game. A ladies' singles event followed in 1884. Wimbledon is the oldest tennis tournament in the world and is still played on grass.

spt-modern-olympics.why: Coubertin admired the role of sport in English schools and knew of earlier revivals, including the Wenlock games in Shropshire and the Zappas games in Greece. In 1894 he called a congress at the Sorbonne, which founded the International Olympic Committee and chose Athens as the first host. A Greek benefactor paid for the stadium.
spt-modern-olympics.impact: The Games have been held every four years since, except during the two world wars. Women first competed in Paris in 1900. The marathon, invented for Athens to recall an ancient legend, became a standard event, and the Games grew into the largest regular gathering of nations in sport.

spt-tour-de-france.why: L'Auto had been set up in 1900 as a rival to the leading sports paper Le Vélo, after a quarrel among its backers linked to the Dreyfus affair. It was losing the circulation battle. A young journalist, Géo Lefèvre, suggested a race around France to the editor Henri Desgrange, longer than anything a competitor had staged.
spt-tour-de-france.impact: Sales of L'Auto rose sharply during the race and Le Vélo closed the following year. The Tour became an annual event, interrupted only by the world wars. High mountain stages were added from 1910 and the leader's yellow jersey in 1919, said to match the colour of the paper's pages.

spt-winter-olympics.why: Figure skating and ice hockey had already appeared at Summer Games, but the Scandinavian countries resisted a separate winter event, fearing it would overshadow their own Nordic Games. As a compromise the International Olympic Committee agreed in 1921 that France, host of the 1924 Paris Games, could stage a winter sports week under its patronage.
spt-winter-olympics.impact: The week was a success and Norway and Finland won most of the medals, which eased Nordic objections. St Moritz hosted the first Games planned as Winter Olympics in 1928. They were held in the same year as the Summer Games until 1992, then moved to a separate four-year cycle from 1994.

spt-world-cup-1930.why: Olympic football had drawn large crowds in 1924 and 1928, both won by Uruguay, but its amateur rules shut out the growing number of professionals. FIFA, led by Jules Rimet, voted to hold its own open tournament. Uruguay won the right to host by offering to pay the visiting teams' costs and build a new stadium.
spt-world-cup-1930.impact: The tournament made a profit and proved the idea could work. It has been held every four years since, apart from 1942 and 1946. Uruguay, offended by the poor European turnout, refused to defend its title in Italy in 1934. The World Cup became the most watched event in football.

spt-jesse-owens.why: Berlin had been awarded the Games in 1931, before the Nazis took power, and the regime turned them into a showcase for its ideology. A campaign for an American boycott narrowly failed. Owens arrived as the favourite, having set several world records in a single afternoon at a college meeting in Michigan the year before.
spt-jesse-owens.impact: His victories were widely taken as a rebuke to Nazi claims of racial superiority. He returned, however, to a segregated United States, received no invitation to the White House and struggled for years to earn a living. Official recognition came late, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1976.

spt-jackie-robinson.why: Since the 1880s an unwritten agreement among club owners had kept Black players out of the major leagues, so they played in separate Negro leagues. After the Second World War, pressure from Black newspapers and campaigners grew. The Dodgers' president Branch Rickey signed Robinson in 1945 and gave him a season in Montreal first.
spt-jackie-robinson.impact: Larry Doby joined the Cleveland Indians a few months later, and other clubs followed slowly, the last not fielding a Black player until 1959. The Negro leagues declined as their best players left. Robinson's debut came before the desegregation of the US armed forces and the main civil rights rulings of the 1950s.

spt-formula-one.why: Grand Prix racing dated from 1906 and a European drivers' championship had run in the 1930s. After the war the sport's governing body defined a new top category called Formula One. A world championship for motorcycles began in 1949, and one for racing drivers was agreed for the following season, linking existing national Grands Prix.
spt-formula-one.impact: The championship gave a scattered set of races a single title to chase, and a constructors' championship was added in 1958. Alfa Romeo dominated the first two seasons and then withdrew. Silverstone still hosts the British Grand Prix, and the series has grown from seven rounds to a worldwide calendar.

spt-bannister-mile.why: The mile record had stood at just over four minutes since 1945, held by the Swede Gunder Hägg. By 1954 the Australian John Landy and the American Wes Santee were both close. Bannister, disappointed by fourth place in the 1500 metres at the 1952 Olympics, set himself the target and applied his medical training to his preparation.
spt-bannister-mile.impact: Landy ran faster the following month, and in August Bannister beat him in Vancouver in a race where both men finished inside four minutes. Bannister retired that year to become a neurologist. More than a thousand runners have since broken four minutes, and the record now stands below 3 minutes 44 seconds.

spt-super-bowl.why: The American Football League had been founded in 1960 as a rival to the long established NFL. The two leagues competed for players, which drove salaries up sharply. In 1966 they agreed to merge, with a championship game between their winners to be played each season until the merger was completed in 1970.
spt-super-bowl.impact: NFL teams won the first two games easily, but the AFL's New York Jets won the third in 1969, which showed the leagues were evenly matched. The name Super Bowl, at first informal, was soon adopted officially. The game became the most watched annual television broadcast in the United States.

spt-rumble-jungle.why: Ali had been stripped of his title in 1967 for refusing the draft during the Vietnam War and was kept out of the ring for more than three years. Foreman, unbeaten, had taken the title from Joe Frazier in 1973. The promoter Don King persuaded Zaire's ruler Mobutu to fund the fight as publicity for his country.
spt-rumble-jungle.impact: Ali held the title until 1978 and the win secured his standing as one of the greatest heavyweights. Foreman retired a few years later, then returned and regained a world title in 1994 at the age of 45. The fight established Don King as boxing's leading promoter.

spt-comaneci.why: Comăneci had been picked out as a small child and trained by Béla and Márta Károlyi within Romania's state sports system. She won the European all-around title in 1975, so she arrived in Montreal as a contender. The scoreboard makers had been advised that a perfect score would not be needed.
spt-comaneci.impact: Her performances made gymnastics one of the most watched Olympic sports and encouraged a trend towards younger, lighter competitors. Concern about that trend later led to the minimum age being raised to sixteen. The 10 point scale itself was replaced in 2006 by an open-ended scoring system.

spt-miracle-on-ice.why: Olympic rules then barred professionals, which kept out NHL players but not the Soviets, who were officially amateurs yet trained full time with state support. The American coach Herb Brooks chose college players and drilled them for months in a fast, passing style. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan weeks earlier had sharpened Cold War feeling.
spt-miracle-on-ice.impact: The game was not the final. The Americans still had to beat Finland two days later to take the gold medal. The win lifted the national mood during a difficult period and raised interest in ice hockey in the United States. NHL professionals were admitted to the Olympics from 1998.

spt-hand-of-god.why: The match was the first meeting of the two sides since the Falklands War of 1982, which gave it an edge well beyond football. Maradona, Argentina's captain, was at the height of his powers. The referee and his linesman did not see the handball, and there was no video review to correct them.
spt-hand-of-god.impact: Maradona said afterwards that the goal was scored a little with his head and a little with the hand of God, which gave it its name. Argentina beat West Germany in the final. The incident remained a standard example in arguments for video assistance, introduced at the World Cup in 2018.

spt-bolt-9-58.why: Bolt was unusually tall for a sprinter and had first specialised in the 200 metres. He took up the 100 metres seriously only in 2008, broke the world record within months, and won the Olympic final in Beijing while slowing before the line. In Berlin he was pushed by the American Tyson Gay and ran flat out.
spt-bolt-9-58.impact: Both Berlin records still stand. Bolt went on to win the 100 and 200 metres at three consecutive Olympic Games, in 2008, 2012 and 2016, before retiring in 2017. His success drew attention and investment to Jamaican sprinting, and he became the best known athlete in track and field.

trd-jiaozi.why: Sichuan used iron rather than copper coins, and a large purchase could require a load too heavy to carry. Private deposit houses issued paper receipts instead, made practical by woodblock printing. Some issuers could not honour their notes, so the state first restricted the business to a group of licensed merchants and then took it over.
trd-jiaozi.impact: Later Chinese governments were tempted to print more notes than they could back, and inflation followed. Under the Mongol Yuan dynasty paper became the main currency, a practice that astonished Marco Polo. The Ming eventually abandoned it for silver. Europe's first banknotes appeared in Sweden in 1661.

trd-medici-bank.why: Florence was already a centre of the wool trade and of banking, though its great houses of the previous century, the Bardi and Peruzzi, had failed in the 1340s. Giovanni had learned the business in a relative's bank in Rome. Handling the papacy's revenues was the most profitable business a banker could win.
trd-medici-bank.impact: The bank opened branches in cities including Venice, Geneva, Bruges and London, each set up as a separate partnership so that one failure would not sink the rest. It declined under Lorenzo the Magnificent through bad loans to rulers and closed in 1494, when the Medici were driven from Florence.

trd-east-india-company.why: Portugal had controlled the sea route round Africa for a century, but Dutch ships began returning from Asia with rich cargoes in the 1590s and prices for pepper rose in London. English merchants feared being shut out. The defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588 had also made long ocean voyages seem less risky.
trd-east-india-company.impact: The first fleet sailed in 1601. Pushed out of the Spice Islands by the Dutch, the company turned to India, trading in cotton cloth and later tea. After its victory at Plassey in 1757 it became a territorial power. The British Crown took over its rule in 1858 after the Indian Rebellion.

trd-voc.why: Several Dutch companies had been sending fleets to Asia since the 1590s, bidding against each other for spices there and undercutting each other at home. The Republic's leading statesman, Johan van Oldenbarnevelt, pressed them to merge. The Dutch were also at war with Spain and wanted a strong weapon against Iberian trade.
trd-voc.impact: The company could wage war, sign treaties and build forts. It founded Batavia, now Jakarta, in 1619 and a supply station at the Cape in 1652, and it came to control much of the spice trade, often by force. It went bankrupt and was dissolved in 1799, leaving its territories to the Dutch state.

trd-tulip-mania.why: Tulips had reached the Netherlands from the Ottoman Empire in the late 1500s. Varieties with flamed petals, later found to be caused by a virus, were rare and prized by wealthy collectors. In the winter of 1636 to 1637 people traded promises to buy bulbs still in the ground, often in taverns and with little money down.
trd-tulip-mania.impact: The courts declined to enforce the contracts and most were settled for a small fraction of the agreed price. Many historians now think the damage to the Dutch economy was limited and that few people were ruined. The story grew through moralising pamphlets and a popular Victorian book on crowd delusions.

trd-bank-of-england.why: England had been at war with France since 1689 and the Crown's credit was poor, so it borrowed at high rates. After the revolution of 1688 Parliament controlled taxation, which made loans to the state safer. Ministers looked to the Dutch, who financed their wars cheaply through public banks and long term debt.
trd-bank-of-england.impact: The government could now borrow large sums at lower interest, which helped Britain outspend richer rivals in the wars of the next century. The bank's notes became the country's paper money and it gradually took on the role of lender to other banks in a crisis. It was nationalised in 1946.

trd-south-sea-bubble.why: The company had been set up in 1711 to take on government debts run up during the War of the Spanish Succession. In 1720 it offered to convert much more of the debt into its own shares. Directors gave shares to politicians and courtiers and lent investors money to buy, which pushed the price up.
trd-south-sea-bubble.impact: A parliamentary inquiry found widespread corruption. Directors had their estates confiscated and the Chancellor of the Exchequer was expelled from the Commons and sent to the Tower. Robert Walpole, who managed the aftermath, rose to dominate government for two decades. New joint-stock companies were restricted by law until 1825.

trd-buttonwood.why: Alexander Hamilton's plan to fund the national debt and create a Bank of the United States had given Americans government bonds and bank shares to trade. Speculation in them ended in a panic in the spring of 1792. Brokers wanted to shut out the auctioneers who dominated sales and to deal with people they could trust.
trd-buttonwood.impact: In 1817 the brokers adopted a formal constitution and rented rooms as the New York Stock and Exchange Board, shortening the name in 1863. The practice of fixed commissions lasted until 1975. The exchange financed canals, railways and industry, and made Wall Street a byword for American finance.

trd-erie-canal.why: The Appalachian Mountains made it slow and costly to move goods between the coast and the interior. The Mohawk valley in New York offered the one low route through. The federal government declined to pay for a canal, so New York State financed it alone, and digging began in 1817.
trd-erie-canal.impact: Tolls repaid the cost of construction within about a decade. Towns along the route such as Buffalo, Rochester and Syracuse grew into cities, settlers moved west and Midwestern grain travelled east. The success set off a canal building boom in other states before railways took over most of the traffic.

trd-corn-laws.why: The laws dated from 1815, when a Parliament of landowners acted to keep out cheap foreign grain after the Napoleonic Wars. They kept bread dear. Manufacturers such as Richard Cobden and John Bright argued that cheaper food and open trade would help workers and exports, and the 1832 Reform Act had given industrial towns more of a voice.
trd-corn-laws.impact: The Conservatives split. Peel's followers, including Gladstone, later joined the Liberals, while the protectionists regrouped under Derby and Disraeli. Repeal came too late to do much for Ireland. From the 1870s cheap grain from North America poured in, which lowered food prices in the towns and hurt British arable farming.

trd-federal-reserve.why: Two earlier national banks had lost their charters, the second after President Andrew Jackson's campaign against it, and many Americans distrusted concentrated financial power. In 1907 the financier J. P. Morgan had to organise a private rescue of the banks. The act was a compromise between bankers who wanted private control and progressives who wanted public oversight.
trd-federal-reserve.impact: The Fed issued a single national paper currency and could lend to banks short of cash. It was widely criticised for failing to stop the bank failures of the early 1930s, and reforms in 1935 concentrated power in the board in Washington. Its interest rate decisions now affect markets worldwide.

trd-bretton-woods.why: Planners blamed the economic chaos of the 1930s, with its competitive devaluations and trade barriers, for deepening the Depression and helping bring about the war. They wanted stable exchange rates without the rigidity of the old gold standard. The United States held most of the world's gold, so the American plan largely prevailed over the British one.
trd-bretton-woods.impact: The International Monetary Fund and World Bank began work soon after the war. Stable exchange rates supported a long period of growth in trade among Western economies. The Soviet Union attended but did not join. Both institutions outlived the fixed rate system and turned increasingly to lending to developing countries.

trd-diners-club.why: Department stores and oil companies already issued charge cards, but each worked only with the firm that issued it. Business entertaining was growing in post-war New York. The wallet story is the company's own account and may be embellished. The new idea was a third party standing between many merchants and their customers.
trd-diners-club.impact: The club made its money from an annual fee and a percentage of each bill paid by the restaurant, the model card networks still use. American Express and Bank of America launched rival cards in 1958, the latter offering revolving credit and later becoming Visa. Plastic soon replaced cardboard.

trd-first-atm.why: British banks then closed in mid-afternoon and customers could get cash only from a cashier. Shepherd-Barron, who worked for the banknote printer De La Rue, said the idea came to him after he arrived at his bank too late, and that he had a chocolate vending machine in mind. Engineers in Britain and Sweden were working on similar machines.
trd-first-atm.impact: Rival designs using a plastic card and a personal identification number, patented in Britain by James Goodfellow, soon became the standard. Machines linked to bank computers let customers draw cash at any hour and from other banks. Banks came to need fewer cashiers, though card and phone payments are now reducing cash use.

trd-nixon-shock.why: Spending on the Vietnam War and domestic programmes had fed inflation, and by 1971 foreign governments held far more dollars than the United States had gold to redeem. The country was heading for its first trade deficit of the century. Nixon and his advisers settled the measures at a private weekend meeting at Camp David.
trd-nixon-shock.impact: An attempt to restore fixed rates at new levels, agreed in Washington that December, broke down by 1973. Major currencies have floated against each other since, and none is tied to gold. The change was followed by a decade of high inflation and by rapid growth in foreign exchange trading.

trd-black-monday.why: Share prices had risen steeply for five years and reached a peak in August 1987. By October investors were uneasy about rising interest rates, a falling dollar and the size of the American trade deficit. Markets had fallen sharply in the preceding week, so sell orders had piled up over the weekend.
trd-black-monday.impact: The Federal Reserve, under its new chairman Alan Greenspan, announced it stood ready to supply cash to the financial system, and markets steadied. American share prices regained their previous peak within two years. Exchanges introduced circuit breakers, rules that halt trading for a time when prices fall too fast.

trd-euro-cash.why: European leaders had agreed a timetable for a single currency at Maastricht in 1992. They wanted to remove exchange rate costs and risks inside the single market and to bind a reunified Germany closely to its neighbours. Countries had to meet limits on inflation, deficits and debt to join. Britain, Denmark and Sweden stayed out.
trd-euro-cash.impact: The old national notes ceased to be legal tender within about two months. Prices became easy to compare across borders and travellers no longer changed money. One central bank in Frankfurt set interest rates for all members, a strain exposed by the debt crisis that began in 2009. The eurozone has since grown to around twenty countries.

trd-lehman.why: During the American housing boom, lenders made risky home loans that banks packaged into securities and sold on. Lehman held large amounts of them and had borrowed heavily. House prices began to fall, another investment bank, Bear Stearns, was rescued in March 2008, and weekend talks to sell Lehman to Barclays or Bank of America failed.
trd-lehman.impact: Lending between banks froze. The insurer AIG was rescued the next day, and within weeks Congress approved a 700 billion dollar fund to support the financial system. A deep worldwide recession followed. Regulators later required banks to hold more capital and to plan for their own orderly failure.

trt-verdun.why: The Franks customarily divided a father's lands among his sons. When the emperor Louis the Pious died in 840, his eldest son Lothair claimed authority over the whole empire. His brothers Charles the Bald and Louis the German allied against him, defeated him at Fontenoy in 841, and forced him to negotiate.
trt-verdun.impact: Lothair kept the imperial title and a long central strip running from the Low Countries to Italy. It had no natural unity and broke up within a generation. Part of it, Lotharingia, later known as Lorraine, was contested by its western and eastern neighbours for the next thousand years.

trt-tordesillas.why: Portugal had spent decades exploring the African coast and held earlier papal grants and a treaty with Castile protecting that route. After Columbus returned, the Spanish-born Pope Alexander VI drew a line that favoured Spain. King John II of Portugal rejected it and negotiated directly with Ferdinand and Isabella to move the line further west.
trt-tordesillas.impact: The Portuguese navigator Cabral reached Brazil in 1500, on their side of the line. Longitude could not be measured accurately, so the boundary was disputed in practice, and a second line was agreed for Asia in 1529. France, England and the Dutch never accepted that two kingdoms could share out the oceans.

trt-westphalia.why: The war began in 1618 with a Protestant revolt in Bohemia against Habsburg rule and widened as Denmark, Sweden and France intervened. Catholic France fought the Catholic Habsburgs, which showed that power mattered as much as faith. By the 1640s all sides were exhausted, and parts of Germany had lost a large share of their people.
trt-westphalia.impact: Calvinism was recognised alongside Catholicism and Lutheranism in the Holy Roman Empire, and the German princes gained wide freedom from the emperor. Swiss independence was acknowledged. France gained territory in Alsace and Sweden on the Baltic coast. War between France and Spain continued until 1659.

trt-utrecht.why: Charles II of Spain died childless in 1700 and left his empire to a grandson of Louis XIV of France. England, the Dutch Republic and Austria went to war to prevent French dominance. By 1711 a new British government wanted peace, and the allies' own candidate had become Holy Roman Emperor, making him just as great a threat.
trt-utrecht.impact: Spain's European possessions were broken up, with the southern Netherlands, Milan and Naples going to Austria under related treaties. France ceded Newfoundland, Acadia and its claims around Hudson Bay to Britain. The idea of a balance of power was written into the settlement. Gibraltar's status is still disputed by Spain.

trt-paris-1783.why: The British surrender at Yorktown in 1781 brought down the government in London and ended Parliament's willingness to pay for the war. Britain was also fighting France and Spain. The prime minister, Lord Shelburne, offered generous terms in the hope of drawing the new nation away from France and keeping its trade.
trt-paris-1783.impact: Florida returned to Spain under a separate treaty. Disputes over unpaid debts, Loyalist property and British forts in the north-west dragged on for a decade. The Native nations who lived on the land between the Appalachians and the Mississippi were not consulted, and American settlement soon pushed into it.

trt-vienna-congress.why: Napoleon had abdicated in April 1814 and the victorious powers, Austria, Russia, Prussia and Britain, met from that autumn to settle the lands he had conquered. They aimed to contain France and restore established dynasties. A quarrel over Poland and Saxony nearly led to war among them, until Napoleon's return from Elba hurried agreement.
trt-vienna-congress.impact: A German Confederation of thirty-nine states replaced the Holy Roman Empire, Prussia gained the Rhineland, Russia took most of Poland and Belgium was joined to the Netherlands. Swiss neutrality was guaranteed. The settlement gave little weight to national feeling, which fuelled the revolutions of 1830 and 1848.

trt-nanking.why: British demand for tea had drained silver to China, which confined foreign trade to the single port of Canton. Opium grown in British India and smuggled in reversed the flow. In 1839 the Chinese official Lin Zexu seized and destroyed the traders' stocks. British steam warships then fought their way up the Yangtze towards Nanjing.
trt-nanking.impact: The treaty did not mention opium, and the trade continued. A follow-up agreement placed British subjects outside Chinese law, and the United States and France soon won similar terms. Shanghai, one of the opened ports, grew into China's largest commercial city. Hong Kong was returned to China in 1997.

trt-guadalupe-hidalgo.why: The United States annexed Texas in 1845 and claimed a border further south than Mexico accepted. President James Polk also wanted California and had offered to buy it. Fighting began in the disputed zone in 1846, and American forces occupied Mexico City the following year. The American envoy negotiated on after being recalled.
trt-guadalupe-hidalgo.impact: The Rio Grande became the border of Texas. Tens of thousands of Mexicans living in the ceded lands were promised citizenship and their property, promises often not kept. In the United States the question of whether slavery would be allowed in the new territories deepened the divisions that led to civil war.

trt-brest-litovsk.why: Russia had suffered enormous losses and its army was falling apart by 1917. The Bolsheviks took power that November promising peace, and agreed an armistice within weeks. Their negotiator Trotsky stalled, hoping for revolution in Germany. In February 1918 the Germans resumed their advance, and Lenin insisted on accepting the terms.
trt-brest-litovsk.impact: Germany moved troops west for its spring offensive of 1918 in France. In Russia the treaty split the Bolsheviks from their coalition partners and helped set off civil war. Soviet forces later retook Ukraine, but Finland, Poland and the Baltic states remained independent between the wars.

trt-munich-agreement.why: Hitler had annexed Austria in March 1938 and then demanded the Sudetenland, home to about three million German speakers and to Czechoslovakia's border fortifications. Memories of the First World War were strong, and British and French leaders judged their forces unready. Chamberlain flew to Germany three times that September to avoid a war.
trt-munich-agreement.impact: Czechoslovakia lost its defences and much of its industry, and Poland and Hungary took territory as well. After Hitler seized Prague, Britain and France guaranteed Poland. The Soviet Union, left out of the talks, moved towards its own pact with Germany. Munich became a byword for the failure of appeasement.

trt-un-charter.why: The League of Nations, which the United States never joined, had failed to prevent a second world war. The Allies had called themselves the United Nations since 1942, and the main powers drafted a plan for a permanent body at Dumbarton Oaks in 1944. The veto for the great powers was settled at Yalta.
trt-un-charter.impact: The Charter created a Security Council with five permanent members holding a veto, a General Assembly of all members and an International Court of Justice. During the Cold War the veto often blocked action. Membership has grown from 51 states to 193, largely through the independence of former colonies.

trt-nato.why: Soviet control had tightened across eastern Europe, with a communist takeover in Czechoslovakia in February 1948 and a blockade of West Berlin from that June. Britain, France and the Benelux countries had signed a defence pact but wanted American backing. Joining broke with the long American tradition of avoiding alliances in peacetime.
trt-nato.impact: The Korean War prompted the allies to build a joint military command under General Eisenhower. West Germany's admission in 1955 was followed within days by the creation of the Warsaw Pact. After the Cold War the alliance took in former communist states, and it now has 32 members.

trt-antarctic-treaty.why: Seven countries claimed parts of Antarctica, and the British, Argentine and Chilean claims overlapped, leading to minor confrontations. The United States and Soviet Union made no claims but reserved the right to. Scientific cooperation during 1957 and 1958 had worked well, and governments wanted to keep Cold War rivalry out of the continent.
trt-antarctic-treaty.impact: The treaty came into force in 1961 and was the first arms control agreement of the Cold War. Any party may inspect another's bases. A protocol agreed in 1991 banned mining and set strict environmental rules. More than fifty countries have now joined.

trt-camp-david.why: Egypt and Israel had fought four wars since 1948, and Israel had occupied the Sinai peninsula since 1967. After the 1973 war President Sadat sought to recover Sinai by negotiation and to align Egypt with the United States. He made a surprise visit to Jerusalem in 1977, but the talks that followed stalled.
trt-camp-david.impact: Israel withdrew from Sinai in stages by 1982. Egypt was suspended from the Arab League for a decade, and Sadat was assassinated by Islamist soldiers in 1981. The second part of the accords, on Palestinian self-rule, was never carried out. The peace between the two states has held.

trt-maastricht.why: The member states had committed in 1986 to complete a single market by the end of 1992, and a committee under Jacques Delors had set out a plan for monetary union. The fall of the Berlin Wall added urgency. France in particular wanted a reunified Germany tied firmly into shared European institutions.
trt-maastricht.impact: Danish voters rejected the treaty in 1992 and accepted it the next year with opt-outs, and French voters approved it only narrowly. Britain secured the right to stay outside the single currency. The treaty added cooperation on foreign policy and justice, and set the budget rules for euro members.

trt-good-friday.why: The conflict over whether Northern Ireland should stay in the United Kingdom or join a united Ireland had killed more than 3,500 people since the late 1960s. Earlier settlements had collapsed. Paramilitary ceasefires from 1994, talks involving Sinn Féin, and new governments in London and Dublin in 1997 created an opening.
trt-good-friday.impact: Northern Ireland gained an assembly and an executive shared between unionists and nationalists. Ireland dropped its constitutional claim to the north, paramilitary prisoners were released and the police service was reformed. The institutions have been suspended several times, but large scale violence has not returned.

trt-paris-climate.why: The Kyoto Protocol of 1997 had set binding targets only for developed countries, and the United States never ratified it. A summit in Copenhagen in 2009 failed to agree a successor. Negotiators then turned to voluntary national pledges covering every country, and a joint announcement by the United States and China in 2014 cleared the way.
trt-paris-climate.impact: The agreement came into force in November 2016. Many governments and companies have since adopted targets to reach net zero emissions. The pledges made so far are not enough to meet the temperature goals, and the United States has withdrawn twice under President Trump, rejoining in between.
